messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Counselor
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Therapy Content: avoid thinking about anything discussed in therapy, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Noah sits stiffly in the chair, his hands clenched so tightly in his lap that his knuckles are white. At nineteen, he should be looking forward to his sophomore year of college, but the future feels like a vast, threatening fog. It has been eight months since he was discharged from the hospital, but in many ways, he feels he never truly left. The illness had come on with a terrifying speed—a headache that bloomed into a raging fever, confusion, and then, nothing. He remembers waking up in the intensive care unit, his body feeling like a foreign country he was trapped inside. The first things he saw were the clear plastic tubes snaking into his arm, the rhythmic pulse of the machines surrounding him, and the sharp, sterile smell of antiseptic that seemed to cling to the back of his throat. For two weeks, that was his world: the constant fear that his body was failing, punctuated by the sharp sting of needles for blood draws and the dispassionate efficiency of the medical staff.

Since coming home, that world has refused to stay in the past. It bleeds into his present in fragments. A few weeks ago, while working his summer job as a camp counselor, he was helping a child with a scraped knee. The moment he tore open the antiseptic wipe, the smell—that clean, chemical hospital smell—hit him, and his heart began to hammer against his ribs. He felt a wave of dizziness so intense he had to grip the edge of a picnic table, convinced he was about to collapse, that the illness was back. He sees the world now as a landscape of hidden threats. He takes a ten-minute detour on his drive to the camp each morning just to avoid passing the hospital. He can’t watch television with his girlfriend anymore if there’s a chance a medical drama might come on; the sight of a syringe or an IV drip is enough to make him break out in a cold sweat. He knows, logically, that he is safe, but he has come to believe his body is an enemy, a traitor that keeps reacting as if the danger is imminent even when his mind knows it isn't.

This feeling of betrayal is worst at night. Sleep offers no escape, only a quiet space for the fear to grow. He lies in the dark, hyper-aware of his own heartbeat, the rhythm of his breathing, cataloging every minor ache or sensation as a potential sign of relapse. He is certain that he can no longer trust his own body to keep him safe. To fend off the terror, he stays up until two or three in the morning, scrolling endlessly on his phone until his eyes burn and he finally passes out from sheer exhaustion. The fatigue makes his job, which he used to love, feel like an impossible task. He is perpetually on edge, and any sudden movement sends a jolt of pure panic through him. Just last week, a child ran up to hug him from behind, and he flinched away with a choked gasp, his body coiled to fight a threat that wasn't there. The look of confusion on the little boy's face has haunted him since.

What frightens him most is the hollowness inside. The plans he had, the person he was before he got sick—it all feels distant and irrelevant. Nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore, just a series of moments to be endured. He came to therapy because his girlfriend, worried and weary of his emotional distance, told him she couldn't watch him disappear anymore. But even this step feels fraught. After their first session, he spent the entire week actively pushing away any thought of what they had discussed, a frantic effort to keep the memories locked down. His immediate problem is the camp’s requirement for an updated physical exam, a form that sits on his desk, untouched. The thought of voluntarily walking into a doctor’s office, of submitting to an examination, feels impossible. Noah is terrified that talking about the illness will somehow make it real again, but a deeper, quieter fear is that he is already broken, and that he will never again feel at home in his own skin.
